tool.name: NetworkX
tool.tagline: Create, analyse and explore graphs and networks in Python
tool.description: NetworkX is the standard pure-Python library for graphs: nodes connected by edges, with attributes on both. It ships hundreds of algorithms for paths, traversal, centrality, communities, flows and DAGs, plus readers and writers for common graph formats. Learn it to model relationships such as social networks, dependencies, road maps and knowledge graphs, and to prototype graph analytics quickly.

glossary.def: One of the things in a graph, such as a person or a city. In NetworkX any hashable value can be a node.
A connection between two nodes in a graph, like a friendship or a road. It can carry attributes such as a weight.
A Python value that can be used as a dict key or set item, such as a number, string or tuple. Lists and dicts are not hashable.
A node that shares an edge with a given node.
The number of edges touching a node. In a directed graph, in-degree counts incoming and out-degree outgoing edges.
A graph whose edges have no direction: an edge between a and b connects both ways, like a handshake.
A graph whose edges point one way, from one node to another, like arrows or one-way streets.
An edge that starts and ends at the same node.
Two or more edges between the same pair of nodes, such as several flights between two cities. Only multigraphs allow them.
A NetworkX graph that allows parallel edges, each told apart by a key.
A number on an edge, such as a distance, cost or strength, that weighted algorithms use instead of counting each edge as 1.
A standard file format for graphs, based on XML, that keeps node and edge attributes.
Exploring a graph layer by layer: first every node one edge away from the start, then two edges away, and so on.
Exploring a graph by going as far as possible along one path before backing up and trying the next.
The standard method for shortest paths when edges have non-negative weights: it always extends the closest unfinished node first.
A path between two nodes with the fewest edges, or with the lowest total weight when weights are used.
A group of nodes that can all reach each other along edges, with no edges to the rest of the graph: one 'island'.
In a directed graph, a group of nodes where each can reach every other by following the arrows.
A directed graph with no cycles: following the arrows never brings you back where you started. Dependencies form DAGs.
An ordering of a DAG's nodes where every node comes after all the nodes pointing to it, such as prerequisites before courses.
A score for how important a node is in a graph; different measures define importance differently.
How many shortest paths between other nodes pass through a node; high for brokers and bottlenecks.
A centrality score where a node is important if important nodes point to it; first used to rank web pages.
In NetworkX, a live, read-only window onto a graph's data, such as G.nodes, that changes when the graph changes.
A part of a graph: some of its nodes and the edges among them.
In a graph, a group of nodes with many edges among themselves and few to the rest.
A score for a split of a graph into communities: how many more edges fall inside communities than chance would give.
The share of a node's neighbour pairs that are also connected to each other, i.e. how many triangles it sits in.
The most that can travel from a source node to a sink node when each edge has a capacity limit.
The cheapest set of edges whose removal disconnects a source from a sink; its total equals the maximum flow.
A set of edges that pairs up nodes, with no node used twice.
A graph with two kinds of nodes, such as people and jobs, where edges only join one kind to the other.
A grid with one row and one column per node, holding the edge weight (or 1) where two nodes are connected and 0 elsewhere.
A matrix built from a graph (degrees minus adjacency) whose eigenvalues reveal components and connectivity.
A way to describe how running time grows with input size: O(n) grows in step with n, O(n²) with its square.
The part of a graph left after repeatedly removing nodes with fewer than k edges.
In NetworkX, an add-on package that runs the same functions with faster code, for example on a GPU or several CPU cores.

concepts.name: Graphs, nodes and edges
concepts.summary: Create a Graph, add nodes and edges, and ask about neighbours, degrees and sizes.
concepts.why: Every NetworkX task starts with building a graph and asking basic questions about it.
concepts.body:
Lots of data is about connections: who is friends with whom, which cities have direct trains, which web pages link to which. Mathematicians call such a network a **graph** (nothing to do with charts). The things in it are **nodes** (also called vertices), and a connection between two nodes is an **edge**. NetworkX is a Python library for building graphs and asking questions about them.

`G = nx.Graph()` creates an empty graph. Any **hashable** Python value can be a node: numbers, strings, tuples, even your own objects. Hashable means it could be a dict key; a list can't be.

Adding structure:

- `G.add_node("a")` and `G.add_nodes_from(["b", "c"])`
- `G.add_edge("a", "b")` adds both nodes automatically if missing
- `G.add_edges_from([("b", "c"), ("c", "d")])`
- `G.remove_node(n)` also removes its edges; `G.remove_edge(u, v)`

Asking about it:

- `G.number_of_nodes()` (or `len(G)`), `G.number_of_edges()`
- `list(G.nodes)`, `list(G.edges)`
- `list(G.neighbors("c"))` or `G["c"]`: the **neighbours** of `c`, the nodes it shares an edge with
- `G.degree("c")`: its **degree**, the number of edges touching it; `dict(G.degree)` for every node
- `G.has_edge("a", "b")`, `"a" in G`

A plain `Graph` is **undirected**: an edge has no direction, like a friendship, so `("a", "b")` is the same edge as `("b", "a")`. It is also simple: adding the same edge twice keeps one edge. An edge from a node to itself, a self-loop, is allowed.

`nx.Graph(edge_list)` builds a graph in one step, and `print(G)` gives a one-line summary such as `Graph with 4 nodes and 3 edges`. The convention is `import networkx as nx`.
concepts.code:
import networkx as nx

G = nx.Graph()
G.add_edge("ana", "ben")
G.add_edges_from([("ben", "cy"), ("cy", "ana"), ("cy", "di")])
G.add_node("eve")                      # isolated node
G.add_edge("ben", "ana")               # duplicate: ignored

print(G)                               # Graph with 5 nodes and 4 edges
print(sorted(G.neighbors("cy")))       # ['ana', 'ben', 'di']
print(G.degree("cy"), dict(G.degree)["eve"])   # 3 0
print(G.has_edge("di", "cy"))          # True (undirected)

G.remove_node("cy")                    # its edges go too
print(G.number_of_edges())             # 1
takeaways: `nx.Graph()` is undirected and simple; any hashable value can be a node
Adding an edge adds its nodes
`G.neighbors`, `G.degree`, `G.has_edge` answer the basic questions
pitfalls: Using a mutable object like a list as a node: nodes must be hashable.

quiz.q: You call G.add_edge(1, 2) twice on an nx.Graph. How many edges are there?
quiz.explain: A simple Graph stores at most one edge between a pair; use MultiGraph for parallel edges.

concepts.name: Node and edge attributes, weights
concepts.summary: Attach data such as weights, names and dates to nodes and edges, and read it back with data=True.
concepts.why: Real networks carry information on nodes and edges, and weighted calculations read it from attributes.
concepts.body:
Every node and edge has an **attribute** dictionary for extra data about it. Set attributes when adding, `G.add_edge("a", "b", weight=4.2, kind="road")` or `G.add_node("a", city="Oslo")`, or later through the views:

- `G.nodes["a"]["city"] = "Bergen"`
- `G.edges["a", "b"]["weight"] = 3.0`, or equivalently `G["a"]["b"]["weight"]`
- `G.graph["name"] = "roads"` for graph-level data

Reading in bulk: `G.nodes(data=True)` yields `(node, attrs)`, `G.edges(data=True)` yields `(u, v, attrs)`, and `G.edges(data="weight", default=1)` yields just one attribute with a fallback. `nx.get_node_attributes(G, "city")` returns a dict, and `nx.set_node_attributes(G, values, "score")` sets many at once (edge versions exist too).

An **algorithm** is a step-by-step method for computing something, such as the shortest route between two nodes. Many NetworkX algorithms can use a **weight** on each edge, a number like a distance or a cost.

Weights are just an attribute, conventionally named `weight`. Weighted algorithms take a `weight=` argument naming which attribute to use, for example `nx.shortest_path(G, s, t, weight="minutes")`. Without it, many algorithms treat every edge as length 1. You can also pass a function `weight=lambda u, v, d: ...` for computed costs.

`G.degree(weight="weight")` gives weighted degree: the sum of the weights of the edges touching the node. Keep attribute names consistent across a graph; missing attributes are a common source of `KeyError`s.
concepts.code:
import networkx as nx

G = nx.Graph(name="trains")
G.add_edge("Oslo", "Bergen", minutes=420, operator="Vy")
G.add_edge("Oslo", "Gol", minutes=180)
G.add_edge("Gol", "Bergen", minutes=200)
G.nodes["Oslo"]["capital"] = True

print(G.edges["Oslo", "Bergen"]["minutes"])        # 420
print(sorted(G.edges(data="operator", default="?")))
# [('Bergen', 'Gol', '?'), ('Oslo', 'Bergen', 'Vy'), ('Oslo', 'Gol', '?')]
print(nx.get_node_attributes(G, "capital"))        # {'Oslo': True}

print(nx.shortest_path(G, "Oslo", "Bergen"))                    # ['Oslo', 'Bergen']
print(nx.shortest_path(G, "Oslo", "Bergen", weight="minutes"))  # ['Oslo', 'Gol', 'Bergen']
print(G.degree("Oslo", weight="minutes"))          # 600
takeaways: Nodes, edges and the graph each carry an attribute dict
`data=True` or `data="attr"` iterates attributes efficiently
Weighted algorithms need `weight="name"`; otherwise edges count as 1
pitfalls: Forgetting `weight=` and getting the path with the fewest hops instead of the lowest cost.

quiz.q: Edges have a 'km' attribute. What does nx.shortest_path(G, a, b) minimise?
options: Nothing; it picks a random path
quiz.explain: Without weight='km', every edge counts as length 1, so it minimises hop count.

concepts.name: Directed graphs and multigraphs
concepts.summary: Choose between Graph, DiGraph, MultiGraph and MultiDiGraph, and use successors, predecessors and in/out degree.
concepts.why: Picking the wrong graph class silently changes results, from degrees to shortest paths.
concepts.body:
NetworkX has four graph classes:

- **Graph**: undirected, at most one edge per pair of nodes. Friendships, road segments.
- **DiGraph**: **directed** edges `u -> v` that point one way, like arrows. Following someone, web links, which task must come before which, one-way streets.
- **MultiGraph**: undirected, and **parallel edges** (several edges between the same pair) are allowed. Several daily flights between two cities.
- **MultiDiGraph**: directed, with parallel edges. Money transfers between accounts, each its own edge; street maps with several routes between two corners.

In a **DiGraph**, `G.successors(n)` gives the nodes `n` points to and `G.predecessors(n)` the nodes pointing to `n`; `neighbors` means successors. `G.in_degree(n)` and `G.out_degree(n)` count each direction. NetworkX functions respect direction: a path must follow the arrows. `G.reverse()` flips every edge, and `G.to_undirected()` drops direction.

In a **multigraph**, each edge has a **key** that tells parallel edges apart: `G.add_edge("A", "B", key="morning", price=99)` returns the key, and `G.edges(keys=True, data=True)` shows them all. Many functions don't support multigraphs or treat parallel edges specially. Converting with `nx.Graph(M)` keeps just one edge per pair and its attributes, possibly not the ones you want, so combine them yourself first if needed (for example, keep the cheapest).

Check a graph's type with `G.is_directed()` and `G.is_multigraph()`.
concepts.code:
import networkx as nx

D = nx.DiGraph([("ana", "ben"), ("ben", "cy"), ("cy", "ana"), ("di", "ana")])
print(sorted(D.successors("ana")), sorted(D.predecessors("ana")))
# ['ben'] ['cy', 'di']
print(D.in_degree("ana"), D.out_degree("ana"))     # 2 1
print(nx.has_path(D, "ana", "di"))                 # False (arrows point to ana)
print(nx.has_path(D.to_undirected(), "ana", "di")) # True

M = nx.MultiGraph()
M.add_edge("OSL", "BGO", key="07:00", price=99)
M.add_edge("OSL", "BGO", key="18:30", price=149)
print(M.number_of_edges("OSL", "BGO"))             # 2
print(sorted(M.edges(keys=True, data="price")))
# [('OSL', 'BGO', '07:00', 99), ('OSL', 'BGO', '18:30', 149)]
print(nx.Graph(M).number_of_edges())               # 1
takeaways: Graph, DiGraph, MultiGraph, MultiDiGraph: direction and parallel edges
DiGraphs have successors/predecessors and in/out degree
Multigraph edges are identified by (u, v, key)
pitfalls: Modelling one-way relationships with an undirected Graph, so paths ignore direction.

quiz.q: In a DiGraph with edge ('a', 'b'), what does list(G.neighbors('b')) contain?
quiz.explain: For DiGraphs, neighbors means successors, and b has no outgoing edges here.

concepts.name: Building graphs from data and files
concepts.summary: Create graphs from edge lists, pandas tables and generators, and read and write formats like edge lists, GraphML and JSON.
concepts.why: Real graphs come from tables and files, and you often need standard test graphs to try ideas on.
concepts.body:
Most graphs start as a table of edges. Ways to load them:

- From a list: `nx.Graph([(u, v), ...])` or `nx.DiGraph(...)`, with attributes as a third dict element, `(u, v, {"weight": 3})`.
- From pandas (a popular library for tables), if you use it: `nx.from_pandas_edgelist(df, source="src", target="dst", edge_attr=["weight"], create_using=nx.DiGraph)`, and back with `nx.to_pandas_edgelist(G)`.
- From a dict of lists or dict of dicts: `nx.Graph({"a": ["b", "c"]})`.

NetworkX can read and write several **file formats** (agreed ways of storing data in a file), in `nx.readwrite`:

- Edge lists: `nx.read_edgelist(path, nodetype=int, data=[("weight", float)])` and `nx.write_edgelist`. Simple, but node attributes are lost and node IDs come back as strings unless you pass `nodetype`.
- **GraphML** (`read_graphml`, `write_graphml`): a format based on XML, a common text format for structured data. It keeps node and edge attributes and opens in graph-drawing apps such as Gephi and Cytoscape.
- **GML**, **GEXF**, Pajek, adjacency lists.
- JSON for drawing graphs on web pages: `nx.node_link_data(G)` and `nx.node_link_graph(data)`.

**Generators** create standard graphs: `nx.complete_graph(5)`, `nx.path_graph(4)`, `nx.grid_2d_graph(3, 3)`, random graphs like `nx.erdos_renyi_graph(n, p, seed=1)` and `nx.barabasi_albert_graph(n, m, seed=1)`, and classic example graphs like `nx.karate_club_graph()`. Pass `seed=` to get the same random graph every time.

**Pickle**, Python's own format for saving objects, is not recommended for long-term storage: it can break between versions. Prefer a standard format.
concepts.code:
import networkx as nx
import pandas as pd

edges = pd.DataFrame({"src": ["a", "b", "c"], "dst": ["b", "c", "a"],
                      "weight": [1.5, 2.0, 0.5]})
G = nx.from_pandas_edgelist(edges, "src", "dst", edge_attr="weight",
                            create_using=nx.DiGraph)
print(G, G["c"]["a"]["weight"])          # DiGraph with 3 nodes and 3 edges 0.5

nx.write_edgelist(G, "g.edgelist", data=["weight"])
H = nx.read_edgelist("g.edgelist", create_using=nx.DiGraph,
                     data=[("weight", float)])
print(sorted(H.edges(data="weight")))    # [('a', 'b', 1.5), ('b', 'c', 2.0), ('c', 'a', 0.5)]

nx.write_graphml(G, "g.graphml")
print(nx.read_graphml("g.graphml").number_of_edges())   # 3

K = nx.karate_club_graph()
print(K.number_of_nodes(), K.number_of_edges())          # 34 78
takeaways: `from_pandas_edgelist` turns edge tables into graphs
GraphML and GEXF keep attributes; edge lists are minimal
Generators give standard and random test graphs; pass `seed=`
pitfalls: Reading an edge list of integers without `nodetype=int`, so nodes '1' and 1 differ.

quiz.q: You read an integer edge list with nx.read_edgelist(path) and G.has_node(1) is False. Why?
options: Nodes were read as strings like '1'; pass nodetype=int
quiz.explain: Without nodetype, node IDs are kept as strings.

concepts.name: Shortest paths
concepts.summary: Find shortest paths and distances, weighted and unweighted, handle unreachable nodes, and compute all-pairs results.
concepts.why: Route planning, degrees of separation ('how many introductions from me to you') and dependency distances are all shortest-path questions.
concepts.body:
`nx.shortest_path(G, source, target)` returns one shortest path as a list of nodes, and `nx.shortest_path_length(G, source, target)` its length. Without a weight, NetworkX uses **breadth-first search** (BFS): it checks every node one edge away, then two, and so on, and the length counts edges. With `weight="km"`, NetworkX uses **Dijkstra's algorithm**, which requires non-negative weights. For negative weights use `nx.bellman_ford_path`, which also detects loops whose total weight is negative.

Variants:

- Leave out `target` to get paths from the source to every reachable node, as a dict.
- `nx.all_shortest_paths(G, s, t)` yields every path that ties for shortest.
- `nx.single_source_dijkstra(G, s, weight=...)` returns distances and paths together.
- `nx.astar_path(G, s, t, heuristic=h, weight=...)` speeds things up on maps, given a function `h` that estimates the remaining distance.
- `dict(nx.all_pairs_shortest_path_length(G))` computes every pair; the work grows with the square of the number of nodes, so only for small graphs.

If the target can't be reached, `shortest_path` raises **`nx.NetworkXNoPath`**; check first with `nx.has_path(G, s, t)` or catch the exception. A missing node raises `nx.NodeNotFound`.

In a DiGraph, paths follow edge direction. `nx.eccentricity`, `nx.diameter` and `nx.average_shortest_path_length` summarize distances but require every node to be reachable from every other (a connected graph).
concepts.code:
import networkx as nx

G = nx.Graph()
G.add_weighted_edges_from([
    ("A", "B", 4), ("A", "C", 1), ("C", "B", 2), ("B", "D", 5), ("C", "D", 8),
], weight="km")
G.add_node("Z")                                       # unreachable

print(nx.shortest_path(G, "A", "D"))                  # ['A', 'B', 'D']  (2 hops)
print(nx.shortest_path(G, "A", "D", weight="km"))     # ['A', 'C', 'B', 'D']
print(nx.shortest_path_length(G, "A", "D", weight="km"))   # 8

dist, paths = nx.single_source_dijkstra(G, "A", weight="km")
print(dist)          # {'A': 0, 'C': 1, 'B': 3, 'D': 8}

try:
    nx.shortest_path(G, "A", "Z")
except nx.NetworkXNoPath as e:
    print("no path:", e)        # no path: No path between A and Z.
takeaways: Unweighted = BFS (counts hops); `weight=` = Dijkstra (non-negative weights)
Unreachable targets raise `NetworkXNoPath`; check with `has_path`
All-pairs work grows with the square of the graph size: small graphs only
pitfalls: Using Dijkstra-based functions with negative weights; use Bellman-Ford instead.

quiz.q: Which algorithm does nx.shortest_path(G, s, t, weight='w') use by default?
quiz.explain: The weighted default method is Dijkstra, which assumes non-negative weights.

concepts.name: Traversal and connected components
concepts.summary: Walk graphs with BFS and DFS, and split them into connected, weakly connected and strongly connected components.
concepts.why: Reachability and components answer 'what is linked to what', and they're the first step in most analyses.
concepts.body:
**Breadth-first search** (BFS) visits nodes in order of distance from a start; **depth-first search** (DFS) goes as deep as possible before backtracking. NetworkX exposes both as iterators, so they stay cheap on large graphs:

- `nx.bfs_edges(G, s)`, `nx.bfs_tree(G, s)`, `nx.bfs_layers(G, s)` (nodes grouped by distance)
- `nx.dfs_preorder_nodes(G, s)`, `nx.dfs_postorder_nodes`, `nx.dfs_edges`
- `nx.descendants(G, s)` and `nx.node_connected_component(G, s)` for everything reachable

**Connected components** split an undirected graph into islands: `nx.connected_components(G)` yields one set of nodes per component, and `nx.number_connected_components(G)` counts them. The largest is `max(nx.connected_components(G), key=len)`, and `G.subgraph(that).copy()` extracts it.

Directed graphs have two notions:

- **Strongly connected**: every node can reach every other following edge directions (`nx.strongly_connected_components`). Cycles of mutual reachability, such as link loops.
- **Weakly connected**: connected if you ignore direction (`nx.weakly_connected_components`).

`nx.condensation(G)` collapses each strongly connected component into one node, producing a DAG of components (a directed graph without loops; next lesson). That's useful for dependency analysis.

Calling `connected_components` on a DiGraph raises an error; use the weak or strong version.
concepts.code:
import networkx as nx

G = nx.Graph([(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (2, 5), (10, 11)])
print(list(nx.bfs_layers(G, 1)))           # [[1], [2], [3, 5], [4]]
print(list(nx.dfs_preorder_nodes(G, 1)))   # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

comps = sorted(nx.connected_components(G), key=len, reverse=True)
print(comps)                               # [{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, {10, 11}]
giant = G.subgraph(comps[0]).copy()
print(giant.number_of_nodes())             # 5

D = nx.DiGraph([("a", "b"), ("b", "c"), ("c", "a"), ("c", "d"), ("e", "d")])
print(sorted(map(sorted, nx.strongly_connected_components(D))))
# [['a', 'b', 'c'], ['d'], ['e']]
print(nx.number_weakly_connected_components(D))   # 1
print(nx.condensation(D).number_of_nodes())       # 3  (a DAG of components)
takeaways: BFS and DFS are lazy iterators; `bfs_layers` groups by distance
Undirected: connected components; directed: strong or weak
`condensation` turns strongly connected components into a DAG
pitfalls: Calling `nx.connected_components` on a DiGraph, which raises NetworkXNotImplemented.

quiz.q: In a DiGraph with edges a->b and b->a plus b->c, which nodes form a strongly connected component of size 2?
quiz.explain: a and b can reach each other; c can't reach back, so it's on its own.

concepts.name: DAGs: topological order and dependencies
concepts.summary: Model dependencies as directed acyclic graphs, order them topologically, find ancestors and cycles, and compute longest paths.
concepts.why: Software build steps, task schedulers, course prerequisites and data pipelines are all DAGs.
concepts.body:
A **directed acyclic graph** (DAG) is a DiGraph with no directed cycles. Use edges `prerequisite -> dependent` and many questions become one-liners:

- `nx.is_directed_acyclic_graph(G)` checks that there are no cycles.
- `list(nx.topological_sort(G))` returns an order in which every node comes after all its prerequisites. It raises `nx.NetworkXUnfeasible` if there's a cycle.
- `nx.topological_generations(G)` groups nodes into layers whose members could all run at the same time, layer by layer.
- `nx.ancestors(G, n)` returns everything `n` depends on, directly or indirectly; `nx.descendants(G, n)` everything that depends on `n`.
- `nx.find_cycle(G)` returns one offending cycle; `nx.simple_cycles(G)` enumerates them all, which can be exponential.
- `nx.dag_longest_path(G, weight="hours")` gives the **critical path**: the chain that determines minimum total duration.
- `nx.transitive_reduction(G)` removes edges implied by others, leaving only direct prerequisites.
- `nx.lexicographical_topological_sort(G)` gives the same order every time, breaking ties alphabetically.

Topological order isn't unique; don't depend on one particular valid order unless you use the lexicographic version. And keep checking for cycles when graphs are edited, because a single back edge makes the whole thing cyclic.
concepts.code:
import networkx as nx

course = nx.DiGraph([
    ("python", "numpy"), ("numpy", "pandas"), ("python", "pandas"),
    ("sql", "pandas"), ("pandas", "dask"), ("numpy", "dask"),
])
print(nx.is_directed_acyclic_graph(course))         # True
print(list(nx.lexicographical_topological_sort(course)))
# ['python', 'numpy', 'sql', 'pandas', 'dask']
print([sorted(g) for g in nx.topological_generations(course)])
# [['python', 'sql'], ['numpy'], ['pandas'], ['dask']]
print(sorted(nx.ancestors(course, "dask")))         # ['numpy', 'pandas', 'python', 'sql']

reduced = nx.transitive_reduction(course)
print(reduced.has_edge("python", "pandas"))         # False (implied via numpy)

course.add_edge("dask", "python")                   # oops: a cycle
try:
    list(nx.topological_sort(course))
except nx.NetworkXUnfeasible:
    print(nx.find_cycle(course)[0])                 # ('python', 'numpy')
takeaways: Edges point from prerequisite to dependent
`topological_sort` orders; `topological_generations` gives layers that can run at the same time
`ancestors`, `transitive_reduction` and `dag_longest_path` answer dependency questions
pitfalls: Relying on one specific topological order when several are valid.

quiz.q: What does nx.transitive_reduction remove from a DAG?
options: Edges whose dependency is already implied by a longer path
quiz.explain: It keeps only direct prerequisites, dropping edges that another path already implies.

concepts.name: Centrality: degree, betweenness, PageRank
concepts.summary: Rank important nodes with degree, closeness, betweenness, eigenvector centrality and PageRank, and know what each one measures.
concepts.why: Finding influencers, bottlenecks and key pages is often the whole point of a network analysis.
concepts.body:
**Centrality** measures how important a node is, and different definitions of importance give different measures. All return a dict `node -> score`.

- **Degree centrality** (`nx.degree_centrality`): the fraction of other nodes it touches directly. Cheap; spots hubs.
- **Closeness** (`nx.closeness_centrality`): based on the average distance to all other nodes. High means it can reach everyone quickly.
- **Betweenness** (`nx.betweenness_centrality`): the fraction of shortest paths between other pairs that pass through the node. Finds **bridges and bottlenecks**, narrow points that much traffic must pass, such as brokers between communities. Its time grows with nodes times edges (written O(nm)), so for large graphs pass `k=500` to sample source nodes and get an approximation.
- **Eigenvector centrality** (`nx.eigenvector_centrality`): important if connected to important nodes.
- **PageRank** (`nx.pagerank(G, alpha=0.85)`): the random-surfer version for directed graphs, robust to dangling nodes. The default choice for link graphs.

Weighted variants take `weight=`. Be careful: in betweenness and closeness the weight is a **distance** (bigger means farther), while in PageRank and eigenvector centrality it's a **strength** (bigger means stronger). Invert weights if needed.

Get the top nodes with `sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)[:5]`. Different measures often disagree, and that disagreement itself is informative.
concepts.code:
import networkx as nx

# Two triangles joined through a single broker node "x"
G = nx.Graph([("a", "b"), ("b", "c"), ("c", "a"),
              ("d", "e"), ("e", "f"), ("f", "d"),
              ("c", "x"), ("x", "d")])

def top(scores, n=2):
    return [k for k, _ in sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:n]]

print(top(nx.degree_centrality(G)))        # ['c', 'd']  (degree 3 each)
bc = nx.betweenness_centrality(G)
print(top(bc, 3))                          # ['x', 'c', 'd']  (all paths cross x)
print(round(bc["x"], 3), bc["a"])          # 0.6 0.0

D = nx.DiGraph([("a", "hub"), ("b", "hub"), ("c", "hub"), ("hub", "a")])
pr = nx.pagerank(D, alpha=0.85)
print(max(pr, key=pr.get))                 # hub
takeaways: Degree = hubs, betweenness = bottlenecks, closeness = reach, PageRank = link importance
Approximate betweenness on big graphs with `k=` samples
Weights mean distance for path-based measures and strength for PageRank
pitfalls: Passing similarity weights (bigger = closer) to betweenness, which treats them as distances.

quiz.q: Which measure best identifies a node that connects two otherwise separate groups?
quiz.explain: Betweenness counts how many shortest paths pass through a node, so brokers score highest.

concepts.name: Views, subgraphs and copies
concepts.summary: Use live views like G.nodes and G.adj, create subgraph and reversed views cheaply, and know when to copy.
concepts.why: Views avoid copying big graphs, but misunderstanding them causes surprising bugs when the original changes.
concepts.body:
`G.nodes`, `G.edges`, `G.adj` and `G.degree` are **views**: read-only, live windows onto the graph's internal dicts. They cost nothing to create and always reflect the current graph, so changing `G` after creating a view changes what the view shows.

**Subgraph views** work the same way:

- `G.subgraph(nodes)`: the induced subgraph on those nodes.
- `G.edge_subgraph(edges)`: only the given edges and the nodes at their ends.
- `G.reverse(copy=False)` for DiGraphs, and `nx.subgraph_view(G, filter_node=f, filter_edge=g)` to filter with your own true/false functions.

These views are frozen: you can't add or remove nodes through them, and they reflect later changes to `G`. Call `.copy()` to get an independent, editable graph, for example `G.subgraph(nodes).copy()`. Note that `copy()` is shallow for attribute values; a mutable value such as a list stored in an attribute is shared. Use `copy.deepcopy` if you will change those.

Don't remove nodes from `G` while iterating over `G.nodes` or a view; it raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`. Collect them first: `G.remove_nodes_from([n for n in G if cond(n)])`.

`nx.relabel_nodes(G, mapping)` renames nodes, returning a copy by default; `nx.freeze(G)` makes a graph immutable.
concepts.code:
import networkx as nx

G = nx.path_graph(6)                      # 0-1-2-3-4-5
sub = G.subgraph([1, 2, 3])               # a view, no copy
print(sorted(sub.edges))                  # [(1, 2), (2, 3)]

G.remove_edge(2, 3)                       # change the original...
print(sorted(sub.edges))                  # [(1, 2)]  ...and the view follows

try:
    sub.add_edge(1, 3)
except nx.NetworkXError as e:
    print(e)                              # Frozen graph can't be modified

own = G.subgraph([1, 2, 3]).copy()        # independent and editable
own.add_edge(1, 3)
print(G.has_edge(1, 3))                   # False

G.remove_nodes_from([n for n in G if G.degree(n) == 0])   # safe bulk removal
big = nx.subgraph_view(G, filter_node=lambda n: n >= 3)
print(sorted(big.nodes))                  # [3, 4, 5]
takeaways: `G.nodes`, `G.edges`, `G.adj` and subgraphs are live, read-only views
Call `.copy()` for an independent, editable subgraph
Don't change a graph while looping over its views
pitfalls: Keeping a subgraph view, then editing the original graph and being surprised the 'copy' changed.

quiz.q: sub = G.subgraph([1, 2]); then G.remove_node(2). What does sub contain?
quiz.explain: A subgraph view reflects the current state of G, so the removed node disappears from it too.

concepts.name: Communities and clustering
concepts.summary: Detect communities with Louvain and label propagation, score the split with modularity, and measure local clustering.
concepts.why: Grouping nodes into tightly knit groups reveals structure such as friend circles, topics and functional modules.
concepts.body:
A **community** is a group of nodes more densely connected to each other than to the rest of the graph. NetworkX's `nx.community` module offers several algorithms, each returning a list of node sets:

- **Louvain** (`nx.community.louvain_communities(G, weight="weight", resolution=1, seed=42)`): greedy modularity optimization in levels. Fast and the usual first choice. Higher `resolution` gives more, smaller communities.
- **Leiden** (`nx.community.leiden_communities`): an improved Louvain that guarantees well-connected communities. It is a recent addition to NetworkX, and add-on packages called backends (a later lesson), such as `nx-cugraph`, speed it up.
- **Label propagation** (`nx.community.label_propagation_communities` or `asyn_lpa_communities`): very fast, but results vary between runs.
- **Greedy modularity** (`greedy_modularity_communities`) and **Girvan-Newman** (`girvan_newman`, which removes high-betweenness edges; slow, small graphs only).

**Modularity** (`nx.community.modularity(G, communities)`) scores a split into communities: the fraction of edges inside communities minus what you'd expect at random. Values above about 0.3 suggest real structure.

Related local measures: the **clustering coefficient** (`nx.clustering(G, n)`, `nx.average_clustering(G)`) is the fraction of a node's neighbour pairs that are themselves connected, i.e. how many triangles it sits in. `nx.triangles(G)` counts them.

Random algorithms need `seed=` for reproducible results.
concepts.code:
import networkx as nx

G = nx.karate_club_graph()                 # the classic 34-member club
parts = nx.community.louvain_communities(G, seed=42)
print(len(parts), sorted(map(len, parts)))   # 4 [4, 6, 10, 14]  (with this seed)
print(round(nx.community.modularity(G, parts), 2))   # 0.43  (edge weights used)

# Compare with the real split after the club broke up
truth = [{n for n, d in G.nodes(data=True) if d["club"] == c}
         for c in ("Mr. Hi", "Officer")]
print(round(nx.community.modularity(G, truth), 2))   # 0.39

print(round(nx.average_clustering(G), 3))  # 0.571
print(nx.triangles(G, 0))                  # 18
takeaways: Louvain is the fast default; set `seed=` for reproducibility
Modularity compares within-community edges to random expectation
Clustering coefficient measures local triangle density
pitfalls: Treating one run of a randomized community algorithm as the definitive answer.

quiz.q: What does increasing the resolution parameter in louvain_communities usually do?
quiz.explain: Higher resolution favours smaller communities in the modularity objective.

concepts.name: Flows, cuts and matchings
concepts.summary: Solve maximum flow and minimum cut problems, and find matchings in bipartite and general graphs.
concepts.why: Capacity planning, assignment problems and network reliability all reduce to flow and matching algorithms.
concepts.body:
**Maximum flow**: in a DiGraph whose edges have a `capacity` attribute, `nx.maximum_flow(G, s, t)` returns the largest amount that can travel from source to sink, plus a dict showing flow on each edge. `nx.maximum_flow_value` returns just the number. Edges without a capacity are treated as infinite.

**Minimum cut**: by the max-flow min-cut theorem, the max flow equals the smallest total capacity of edges whose removal separates s from t. `nx.minimum_cut(G, s, t)` returns that value and the two node sets, revealing the narrowest point. For unweighted reliability questions, `nx.minimum_edge_cut` and `nx.node_connectivity` tell you how many edges or nodes must fail to disconnect the graph.

**Min-cost flow** (`nx.min_cost_flow`, `nx.network_simplex`) adds a `weight` (cost) per unit and `demand` on nodes, for cheapest shipping plans.

**Matching** pairs up nodes with no node used twice:

- **Bipartite** graphs, with two kinds of nodes and edges only between kinds, like people and jobs: `nx.bipartite.maximum_matching(G, top_nodes=workers)` (Hopcroft-Karp), and `nx.bipartite.minimum_weight_full_matching` for the assignment problem with costs.
- General graphs: `nx.max_weight_matching(G)` returns a set of edges.

Matchings come back as dicts mapping both directions (bipartite) or sets of pairs (general), so read the docs for each function's format.
concepts.code:
import networkx as nx

G = nx.DiGraph()
G.add_edge("s", "a", capacity=10)
G.add_edge("s", "b", capacity=5)
G.add_edge("a", "b", capacity=15)
G.add_edge("a", "t", capacity=4)
G.add_edge("b", "t", capacity=9)

value, flow = nx.maximum_flow(G, "s", "t")
print(value, flow["s"]["a"] + flow["s"]["b"])   # 13 13
cut_value, (reach, rest) = nx.minimum_cut(G, "s", "t")
print(cut_value, sorted(reach))                 # 13 ['a', 'b', 's']  (cut a->t, b->t)

B = nx.Graph()
workers, jobs = ["ana", "ben", "cy"], ["cook", "drive", "fix"]
B.add_edges_from([("ana", "cook"), ("ana", "drive"), ("ben", "cook"), ("cy", "fix")])
m = nx.bipartite.maximum_matching(B, top_nodes=workers)
print({w: m[w] for w in workers if w in m})
# {'ana': 'drive', 'ben': 'cook', 'cy': 'fix'}
takeaways: Max flow = min cut: the cut shows the bottleneck edges
Edges need a `capacity` attribute; missing means infinite
Use bipartite matching for assignment problems
pitfalls: Forgetting capacities on some edges, which makes them infinite and the flow unbounded.

quiz.q: The maximum flow from s to t is 13. What is the total capacity of the minimum s-t cut?
quiz.explain: The max-flow min-cut theorem says the two values are always equal.

concepts.name: Graphs as matrices
concepts.summary: Convert graphs to NumPy and SciPy sparse adjacency matrices, use Laplacians and spectra, and go back from matrices to graphs.
concepts.why: Matrix form connects graphs to linear algebra and machine learning, and is how fast numerical code handles them.
concepts.body:
A **matrix** is a grid of numbers, like a table. A graph with n nodes can be written as an n x n **adjacency matrix** A, where `A[i, j]` is the weight of edge i-j (or 1), and 0 otherwise.

- `nx.to_numpy_array(G, nodelist=order, weight="weight")` gives a dense NumPy array (NumPy is Python's main library for grids of numbers). Fine for up to a few thousand nodes.
- `nx.to_scipy_sparse_array(G, nodelist=order)` gives a SciPy sparse array, which stores only the non-zero entries: the right choice for large graphs with relatively few edges.
- `nx.from_numpy_array(A)` and `nx.from_scipy_sparse_array(S)` go back; nodes are numbered 0 to n-1, so relabel afterwards if needed.

Pass `nodelist=` to control row order; otherwise it follows `G.nodes` insertion order, which is easy to get wrong when matching rows to nodes.

Matrix powers count walks: `(A @ A)[i, j]` is the number of 2-step walks from i to j. The **Laplacian** `L = D - A` (`nx.laplacian_matrix(G)`) underlies spectral methods. The number of zero eigenvalues of L equals the number of connected components, and the second-smallest eigenvalue, the **algebraic connectivity** (`nx.algebraic_connectivity`), measures how well connected the graph is. Its eigenvector (Fiedler vector) gives a classic way to split a graph in two.

`nx.adjacency_spectrum`, `nx.laplacian_spectrum` and `nx.normalized_laplacian_matrix` are available too. These need NumPy and SciPy installed.
concepts.code:
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np

G = nx.Graph([("a", "b"), ("b", "c"), ("c", "a"), ("d", "e")])
order = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]

A = nx.to_numpy_array(G, nodelist=order)
print(A[0].tolist())                       # [0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]
print(int((A @ A)[0, 0]))                  # 2  (a->b->a and a->c->a)

S = nx.to_scipy_sparse_array(G, nodelist=order)
print(type(S).__name__, S.nnz)             # csr_array 8

L = nx.laplacian_matrix(G, nodelist=order).toarray()
eig = np.linalg.eigvalsh(L)
print(int(np.sum(np.isclose(eig, 0))))     # 2  (= number of components)

H = nx.from_numpy_array(A)
print(sorted(H.edges)[:2])                 # [(0, 1), (0, 2)]  (integer labels)
takeaways: Dense arrays for small graphs, SciPy sparse arrays for large ones
Always pass `nodelist=` to fix the row order
Laplacian spectra reveal components and connectivity
pitfalls: Building a dense adjacency matrix for a million-node graph and running out of memory.

quiz.q: A graph's Laplacian has three eigenvalues equal to zero. What does that tell you?
quiz.explain: The multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue equals the number of connected components.

concepts.name: Inside the graph data structure
concepts.summary: Understand NetworkX's dict-of-dicts adjacency, its memory and speed costs, and how to subclass graphs with custom dict factories.
concepts.why: Knowing the representation explains why NetworkX is flexible but memory-hungry, and which operations are cheap.
concepts.body:
A NetworkX `Graph` is a set of nested Python dicts:

- `G._node`: node -> node attribute dict
- `G._adj`: node -> {neighbour -> edge attribute dict}, a **dict of dicts of dicts**
- `G.graph`: graph attributes

In an undirected graph, the edge attribute dict is shared: `G._adj[u][v] is G._adj[v][u]`, so changing an attribute through either side updates both. A DiGraph keeps two structures, `_succ` and `_pred` (with `_adj` aliasing `_succ`), so it can answer predecessor queries quickly at roughly double the memory. Multigraphs add one more level, keyed by edge key.

Consequences:

- Adding, removing and testing nodes and edges, and iterating neighbours, are all O(1) or O(degree), and anything hashable can be a node.
- Memory is high: each edge costs a few hundred bytes of dict overhead, so 100 million edges is far beyond a typical machine. Libraries with compact array storage use a fraction of that.
- Algorithms are pure Python loops, so they run much slower than compiled implementations on large graphs.

The classes are designed for subclassing. Class attributes such as `node_dict_factory`, `adjlist_outer_dict_factory`, `adjlist_inner_dict_factory` and `edge_attr_dict_factory` let you swap the dict types, for example to use ordered or disk-backed mappings. The views (`G.adj`, `G.nodes`) are thin read-only wrappers over these dicts.
concepts.code:
import sys
import networkx as nx

G = nx.Graph()
G.add_edge("a", "b", weight=3)
print(G._adj)                       # {'a': {'b': {'weight': 3}}, 'b': {'a': {'weight': 3}}}
print(G._adj["a"]["b"] is G._adj["b"]["a"])   # True: one shared attribute dict
G["a"]["b"]["weight"] = 7
print(G["b"]["a"]["weight"])        # 7

D = nx.DiGraph([("a", "b")])
print(D._succ, D._pred)             # {'a': {'b': {}}, 'b': {}} {'a': {}, 'b': {'a': {}}}
print(D._adj is D._succ)            # True

class TinyAttrGraph(nx.Graph):
    edge_attr_dict_factory = dict   # swap in any MutableMapping type here

big = nx.gnm_random_graph(2_000, 20_000, seed=1)
per_edge = sum(sys.getsizeof(nbrs) + sum(sys.getsizeof(d) for d in nbrs.values())
               for nbrs in big._adj.values()) / big.number_of_edges()
print(per_edge > 100)               # True: hundreds of bytes per edge
takeaways: Graphs are nested dicts: node -> neighbour -> attribute dict
Undirected edges share one attribute dict; DiGraphs store succ and pred
Flexible and O(1) updates, but heavy memory and pure-Python speed
pitfalls: Loading a 100-million-edge graph into NetworkX without estimating its dict overhead first.

quiz.q: Why does a DiGraph use roughly twice the adjacency memory of a Graph with the same edges stored once?
options: It keeps both successor and predecessor dicts
It uses lists instead of dicts
quiz.explain: _succ and _pred both index every edge so predecessors can be found in O(1).

concepts.name: Algorithm cost and scaling strategies
concepts.summary: Estimate algorithm complexity, use approximations and sampling, and decide when to move to igraph, graph-tool, a graph database or GPU.
concepts.why: Many NetworkX analyses work on 10,000 nodes and never finish on 10 million; experts choose the right tool before starting.
concepts.body:
Know the cost before you run something. **Big-O notation** describes how running time grows with graph size, where n is the number of nodes and m the number of edges:

- Linear, O(n + m): BFS, DFS, components, degree, topological sort, PageRank per iteration. Fine up to millions of edges, if slowly in pure Python.
- O(m + n log n) per source: Dijkstra. All-pairs shortest paths multiplies that by n.
- O(nm): exact betweenness and closeness. Hours or days on million-edge graphs.
- Exponential: simple cycles, all simple paths, cliques, isomorphism and exact colouring on hard instances.

Strategies, in order:

- **Reduce the graph**: take the largest component, remove low-degree nodes or edges under a weight threshold, or analyse a k-core (`nx.k_core`).
- **Sample and approximate**: `betweenness_centrality(G, k=500, seed=1)`, the `nx.approximation` module (clique, diameter, treewidth, max independent set), and early cutoffs such as `cutoff=` on path functions.
- **Use a backend**: dispatch to `nx-cugraph` (GPU) or `nx-parallel` with the same code (next lesson).
- **Switch tools**: igraph and graph-tool (C/C++ cores), rustworkx (Rust), GraphFrames on Spark, or a graph database such as Neo4j for interactive queries on huge, changing graphs.

Measure with `time.perf_counter()` on growing subgraphs and extrapolate before launching a full run. A doubling of n turning 1 minute into 4 is quadratic behaviour.
concepts.code:
import time
import networkx as nx

def timed(f, *a, **kw):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = f(*a, **kw)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

G = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(2_000, 3, seed=7)

exact, t_exact = timed(nx.betweenness_centrality, G)
approx, t_approx = timed(nx.betweenness_centrality, G, k=200, seed=7)

top = lambda s: set(sorted(s, key=s.get, reverse=True)[:10])
print(len(top(exact) & top(approx)) >= 7)   # True: top-10 mostly agree
print(t_exact > 3 * t_approx)               # True: sampling is much faster

core = nx.k_core(G, k=4)                    # shrink before heavy analysis
print(core.number_of_nodes() < G.number_of_nodes())   # True
print(nx.approximation.diameter(G) <= 8)    # True: 2-sweep lower bound, fast
takeaways: Know the complexity class before running an algorithm on a big graph
Reduce, sample or approximate first; `k=` for betweenness
Switch to backends, compiled libraries or graph databases at scale
pitfalls: Starting `all_simple_paths` or exact betweenness on a large graph without estimating run time.

quiz.q: Exact betweenness takes 10 minutes on 50,000 nodes. Roughly how long on a similar 100,000-node graph with twice the edges?
quiz.explain: Brandes' algorithm is O(nm); doubling both n and m roughly quadruples the time.

concepts.name: Backends and dispatching
concepts.summary: Run NetworkX algorithms on accelerated backends like nx-cugraph and nx-parallel through the dispatch system, without rewriting code.
concepts.why: Backends let existing NetworkX code run on GPUs or many cores, often 10 to 100 times faster, with a configuration change.
concepts.body:
Since NetworkX 3.2 many functions are **dispatchable**: when called, NetworkX can hand the work to an installed **backend** package that implements the same function signature with faster code.

Notable backends:

- **nx-cugraph** (NVIDIA RAPIDS): GPU implementations of PageRank, betweenness, Louvain, Leiden, shortest paths and more.
- **nx-parallel**: CPU multiprocessing with joblib for algorithms such as betweenness and all-pairs computations.
- **graphblas-algorithms**: sparse linear-algebra implementations using GraphBLAS.

Ways to use one:

- Per call: `nx.betweenness_centrality(G, backend="parallel")`.
- Automatically: set `nx.config.backend_priority.algos = ["cugraph"]` or the environment variable `NX_CUGRAPH_AUTOCONFIG=True`, and existing code dispatches to the backend where supported, falling back to NetworkX otherwise.
- With backend graph objects: functions called on a backend's own graph type dispatch to that backend automatically.

Converting a NetworkX graph to a backend's format costs time, so NetworkX can **cache** converted graphs on `G.__networkx_cache__` (`nx.config.cache_converted_graphs`). Changing the graph through the normal methods clears the cache.

`nx.config.backends` lists installed backends, and the docs mark which functions each backend supports. Logging (`networkx` logger at DEBUG) shows which implementation actually ran.
concepts.code:
import networkx as nx

print(sorted(nx.config.backends))       # e.g. ['cugraph', 'parallel'] when installed; [] otherwise
print(nx.config.cache_converted_graphs)  # True

G = nx.karate_club_graph()
# Explicitly ask for the built-in implementation ("networkx" is always available)
pr = nx.pagerank(G, backend="networkx")
print(max(pr, key=pr.get))               # 33

# With nx-parallel installed, the same call could run on all cores:
#   nx.betweenness_centrality(G, backend="parallel")
# With nx-cugraph installed, route supported calls to the GPU automatically:
#   nx.config.backend_priority.algos = ["cugraph"]
try:
    nx.pagerank(G, backend="no-such-backend")
except ImportError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)              # ImportError (unknown backend)
takeaways: Dispatchable functions can run on installed backends unchanged
Choose per call with `backend=` or globally via `nx.config.backend_priority`
Converted graphs are cached; check logs for which backend ran
pitfalls: Assuming every function is accelerated: unsupported ones silently fall back to pure Python.

quiz.q: You set nx.config.backend_priority.algos = ['cugraph'] and call a function nx-cugraph doesn't implement. What happens?
options: NetworkX falls back to its own implementation
The GPU emulates it on CPU
quiz.explain: Automatic dispatch only uses backends that support the function; otherwise NetworkX runs its own version.
